name: trailing_comma/array_one_line
why: The comma is not needed, so it goes and its (empty) fodder moves to the ].

name: trailing_comma/array_multiline_missing
why: A newline before the ] means the comma has to be added.

name: trailing_comma/array_multiline_present
why: Already right: nothing moves, nothing is added. The no-op is graded too.

name: trailing_comma/array_comment_before_comma
why: Removing the comma must not take the comment with it: it moves to the front of the close fodder.

name: trailing_comma/array_comma_on_its_own_line
why: The middle branch of fixComma: the comma is needed but a newline separates it from the element, so that newline moves to the ] and merges with the one already there.

name: trailing_comma/array_comment_only_before_close
why: An interstitial is not a newline, so no comma is added. This is what containsNewline is for.

name: trailing_comma/array_line_comment_before_close
why: A line-end comment does contain a newline, so a comma is added before it.

name: trailing_comma/array_empty
why: Upstream returns before the base traversal, so the close fodder is not even visited.

name: trailing_comma/array_empty_multiline
why: A newline before the ], but no element to put a comma after. Must not add one.

name: trailing_comma/array_nested
why: One array losing a comma while the other gains one, in one traversal.

name: trailing_comma/object_one_line
why: The object half of the same rule.

name: trailing_comma/object_multiline_missing
why: The comma is added to the last field, not to the object.

name: trailing_comma/object_last_field_is_a_local
why: The last field can be an ObjectLocal, whose CommaFodder is the slot that has to be found.

name: trailing_comma/object_last_field_is_an_assert
why: And it can be an assert, which has no Expr1 at all.

name: trailing_comma/object_empty
why: The early return again, for the object hook.

name: trailing_comma/array_comp_comma
why: A comprehension's comma is always removed, however it is laid out, and its fodder goes to the front of the for.

name: trailing_comma/array_comp_comma_multiline
why: Still removed when the comprehension spans lines — this is removeComma, not fixComma.

name: trailing_comma/array_comp_comment_before_comma
why: The comment lands in the ForFodder, where unparseSpecs writes it before the for.

name: trailing_comma/array_comp_no_comma
why: Nothing to remove.

name: trailing_comma/object_comp_comma
why: The object comprehension takes the last field's CommaFodder, not a TrailingCommaFodder — upstream never fills that slot on an ObjectComp.

name: trailing_comma/object_comp_with_local
source: { local v = 1, [k]: v, for k in ['a'] }
why: The last field is still the computed one, so the local's comma is untouched.

name: trailing_comma/apply_arguments_are_untouched
why: This pass handles arrays, objects and comprehensions only. An argument list's trailing comma is FixNewlines' business, and must not move here.

name: trailing_comma/function_params_are_untouched
why: Same, for a parameter list.

name: slice_colon/double_colon
why: `::` is one operator token, so StepColonFodder is never filled and this is already the tree a[:] produces. Nothing for the pass to do.

name: slice_colon/empty_step
why: Two adjacent colons again, so still nothing in the slot.

name: slice_colon/comment_before_step_colon
why: The case the pass exists for: the colon is about to disappear, so the comment before it has to move to the ] first.

name: slice_colon/newline_before_step_colon
why: A LineEnd in the slot rather than an interstitial.

name: slice_colon/comment_with_a_real_step
why: There is a step, so the colon stays and so does its fodder.

name: slice_colon/plain
why: No step colon at all.

name: slice_colon/all_three
why: Nothing redundant.

name: pretty_names/index_single_quoted
why: The plain case: brackets to a dot.

name: pretty_names/index_double_quoted
why: The string's kind does not matter, only its value.

name: pretty_names/index_verbatim
why: A verbatim string's value is already collapsed, so it is an identifier too.

name: pretty_names/index_not_an_identifier
why: Left alone.

name: pretty_names/index_empty_string
why: IsValidIdentifier's first guard.

name: pretty_names/index_keyword
why: IsValidIdentifier ends by asking the keyword table, so this keeps its brackets.

name: pretty_names/index_keyword_cased
why: But only the keywords exactly: this one is promoted.

name: pretty_names/index_leading_digit
why: isIdentifierFirst rejects a digit.

name: pretty_names/index_escape_sequence
why: A fully escaped string keeps its escapes in Value, so the pass is asked about the text `fo\u006f` and refuses it. Do not 'fix' this by unescaping first.

name: pretty_names/index_block_string
why: A block string's value ends in a newline, so it is never an identifier.

name: pretty_names/index_number
why: Not a string at all.

name: pretty_names/index_comment_before_bracket
why: THE ODDITY: RightBracketFodder is assigned over rather than moved into, and that one slot doubles as the fodder before the identifier — so tk fmt drops this comment. The oracle is what confirms it.

name: pretty_names/index_comment_before_string
why: This one survives, as the literal's own fodder becoming the id fodder.

name: pretty_names/index_comment_both_sides
why: Both at once, so the oracle says which of the two is kept.

name: pretty_names/super_index_is_untouched
why: SuperIndex has the same Id/Index shape as Index and this pass does NOT override it, so super['foo'] keeps its brackets. Worth pinning: tidying it would be a divergence.

name: pretty_names/field_computed_string
why: Both steps in one visit: ObjectFieldExpr to ObjectFieldStr to ObjectFieldID.

name: pretty_names/field_computed_not_an_identifier
why: The first step has no identifier check, so the brackets go and the quotes stay.

name: pretty_names/field_computed_expression
why: Not a literal string, so neither step applies.

name: pretty_names/field_computed_comments_everywhere
why: Both FodderMoveFront calls at once: Fodder1 into the literal's own fodder, Fodder2 into the OpFodder. This is the snippet that says whether the port got the direction of each move right.

name: pretty_names/field_computed_method
why: The method branch moves Fodder2 into ParenLeftFodder instead of into OpFodder.

name: pretty_names/field_quoted
why: Only the second step.

name: pretty_names/field_quoted_keyword
why: Stays quoted. tests/golden/issue195.jsonnet in the corpus is this case.

name: pretty_names/field_hidden
why: Visibility has to survive the kind change.

name: pretty_names/field_super_sugar
why: And so does +:.

name: pretty_names/field_local_and_assert
source: { local x = 1, assert true, a: x }
why: Neither kind has a name expression, so both must be left exactly alone.

name: pretty_names/nested
why: The traversal has to keep working after the rewrite, since upstream calls the base traversal on the changed node.

name: string_style/double_to_single
why: The plain case, and the one the default option asks for: StringStyleSingle with nothing to avoid.

name: string_style/already_single
why: Already right. A no-op that still goes through StringUnescape and StringEscape, so it grades the round trip.

name: string_style/empty
why: Nothing to count, so the style decides alone.

name: string_style/block_string
why: The first of three early returns: a block string is never restyled, whatever it holds.

name: string_style/block_string_with_both_quotes
why: And the early return is unconditional, so a block string holding both quotes is not even examined.

name: string_style/verbatim_single
why: The second early return.

name: string_style/verbatim_double
why: The third.

name: string_style/verbatim_doubled_quote
why: A verbatim string's Value has its doubled quotes already collapsed, so restyling it would need re-doubling. Upstream does not try: it returns.

name: string_style/single_quote_inside_double
why: numSingle > 0 forces useSingle false, which is what it already is. The value round-trips unchanged, so this must be a no-op.

name: string_style/single_quote_inside_single
why: The carve-out doing work: the escape is what the quote choice is avoiding, so this becomes a double-quoted string with no escape at all.

name: string_style/double_quote_inside_single
why: numDouble > 0 forces useSingle true. Already single, already unescaped: a no-op.

name: string_style/double_quote_inside_double
why: The carve-out overriding the option in the other direction: StringStyleSingle wanted single anyway, and here it is the escapes that make it worth doing.

name: string_style/both_quotes_in_double
why: Both present, so neither syntax avoids escaping and upstream returns without touching it. The kind stays Double even though the option says Single.

name: string_style/both_quotes_in_single
why: The same refusal from the other side.

name: string_style/escaped_single_quote_in_double
why: A needless escape: \' is legal in a double-quoted string, and numSingle > 0 keeps the kind Double, so only the value changes. The one snippet where the kind is untouched and the text is not.

name: string_style/escaped_double_quote_in_single
why: The mirror image, and here the kind changes too even though it was already Single-shaped.

name: string_style/escape_newline
why: StringEscape writes \n back, so the value survives and only the kind moves.

name: string_style/escape_tab
why: Same for \t.

name: string_style/escape_backslash
why: And for the backslash, which is the escape that would compound if the round trip were wrong.

name: string_style/escape_solidus
why: \/ is accepted by StringUnescape (see json.org) and never written back by StringEscape, so the escape is silently dropped.

name: string_style/escape_unicode_ascii
why: An escape collapsing to a plain character: \u0041 is A, and StringEscape leaves A alone.

name: string_style/escape_unicode_latin1
why: So does e-acute, which is above the C1 range StringEscape re-escapes.

name: string_style/escape_unicode_c1
why: But U+009F is inside it, so the escape comes back — in lower case, because StringEscape formats with %04x. A case change with no other difference.

name: string_style/escape_nul
why: The one character StringEscape spells out explicitly rather than by range.

name: string_style/non_ascii_literal
why: A character written as itself rather than escaped stays that way.

name: string_style/import
why: THE REASON THIS PASS OVERRIDES LiteralString AND NOT Visit: Base.Import reaches the filename through the LiteralString hook only, so a pass overriding Visit would miss every import in the file.

name: string_style/import_str
why: Same route, different hook on the way in.

name: string_style/import_bin
why: And the third.

name: string_style/import_already_single
why: The no-op, so the import path is graded in both directions.

name: string_style/field_name
why: A field name is a LiteralString like any other. In the pipeline PrettyFieldNames has already unquoted this one; in isolation the pass still restyles it.

name: string_style/field_name_keyword
why: The pipeline case: PrettyFieldNames leaves a keyword quoted, so this pass is what decides which quote it keeps. tests/golden/issue195.jsonnet is exactly this.

name: string_style/computed_field_name
why: Reached through Visit rather than through the field kind, since ObjectFieldExpr's name is an ordinary expression.

name: string_style/index
why: And an index's string, which PrettyFieldNames would have promoted first.

name: string_style/nested
why: Several literals in one traversal, in three different positions.

name: comment_style/hash_to_slash
why: The plain case: CommentStyleSlash rewrites the leading # as //, keeping everything after it.

name: comment_style/hash_no_space
why: The rewrite is textual — "//" + comment[1:] — so there is no space to preserve.

name: comment_style/hash_empty
why: A bare hash. len(*comment) > 1 fails, so the hashbang guard is not even consulted.

name: comment_style/double_hash
why: Only the first character is replaced, so a doubled hash becomes //# and not //.

name: comment_style/slash_left_alone
why: Already slash: the branch asks for comment[0] == '#' and this is not it.

name: comment_style/hashbang_first
why: The documented carve-out: a #! in the file's first fodder is left alone.

name: comment_style/hashbang_bare
why: The shortest comment the guard can fire on: len 2, and comment[1] is '!'.

name: comment_style/hashbang_with_a_space
why: Not a hashbang: the guard reads comment[1], which is a space here, so this is rewritten.

name: comment_style/hashbang_twice
why: AN ODDITY, AND WHY seenFirstFodder IS THE STATE IT IS: the guard returns *before* setting seenFirstFodder, so a second #! is still 'first' and is also spared.

name: comment_style/hashbang_after_a_comment
why: An ordinary comment does set seenFirstFodder, so the #! after it is rewritten to //!.

name: comment_style/hashbang_after_interstitial
why: seenFirstFodder is assigned inside the `Kind != FodderInterstitial` branch, so an interstitial does not count as having been seen and the #! after it is still spared. Note the #! has to be on the SAME line: a newline between them would emit its own commentless LineEnd, and that would set the flag.

name: comment_style/hashbang_after_paragraph
why: Converted, and not for the obvious reason. addFodderSafe puts a synthetic commentless LineEnd in front of a paragraph appended to empty fodder (the FodderAppend rule src/lexer.rs documents), and it is that element which sets the flag before the paragraph is ever examined.

name: comment_style/hashbang_after_blank_line
why: THE FLAG IS SET OUTSIDE THE len(Comment) == 1 CHECK: a leading newline is a commentless LineEnd, nothing about it can be rewritten, and it still counts as fodder seen — so one blank line at the top of a file disables the hashbang carve-out.

name: comment_style/interstitial_c_comment
why: An interstitial has to be a C comment, so under CommentStyleSlash there is nothing to do — and the element must not set the flag either.

name: comment_style/paragraph_c_comment
why: len(Comment) is 2, so the rewrite is skipped entirely. A multi-line comment is never restyled, in either direction.

name: comment_style/two_hash_lines
why: Two elements, each with one comment: both rewritten, and neither merged into the other.

name: comment_style/hash_mid_file
why: Not every comment is at the top of the file; this one is in an object field's comma fodder.

name: comment_style/hash_in_final_fodder
why: Base.File visits the final fodder after the root node, so a trailing comment is reached.

name: comment_style/hash_in_in_super_fodder
why: A TRAVERSAL HOLE WITH A VISIBLE CONSEQUENCE: Base.InSuper visits only the index, so InFodder is never reached and this # survives tk fmt.

name: comment_style/hash_in_index_id_fodder
why: The second hole: Index's RightBracketFodder doubles as the fodder before an identifier, and Base.Index skips it when Id is set. So this # survives too.

name: comment_style/hash_in_super_index_id_fodder
why: The contrast that makes the previous one a hole rather than a rule: Base.SuperIndex visits IdFodder unconditionally, so the same comment in the same position is rewritten here.

name: comment_style/hash_in_parameter_eq_fodder
why: EqFodder is visited only where the parameter has a default, and this one does, so the comment is reached. Without the default there is no = for a comment to sit before.

name: comment_style/hashbang_after_slash_comment
why: A comment already in the target style is not rewritten but does set the flag, so the #! after it is converted. The pair with hashbang_after_interstitial: what matters is the element's kind, not whether anything changed.

name: max_blank_lines/three_blanks_between_fields
why: Four newlines are one LineEnd with blanks=3, clamped to 2. The base case.

name: max_blank_lines/exactly_two_blanks
why: blanks == MaxBlankLines, so the strict `>` leaves it. A graded no-op.

name: max_blank_lines/one_blank
why: Under the limit. No-op.

name: max_blank_lines/ten_blanks
why: A long run collapses to exactly 2, not to 2 per newline: blanks is a count on one element, not a run of elements.

name: max_blank_lines/leading_blanks
why: The file's opening fodder. In the pipeline removeInitialNewlines (step 2) deletes this before the pass (step 3) can see it; the oracle runs each pass on a fresh parse, so here it is clamped instead. That difference is the whole reason those two steps' order is load-bearing.

name: max_blank_lines/trailing_blanks_in_final_fodder
why: base::file visits the final fodder, so it is clamped to 2 — and then removeExtraTrailingNewlines (step 14) zeroes it anyway. Both steps touch this one element, in that order.

name: max_blank_lines/blanks_after_a_paragraph_comment
why: A Paragraph carries the blanks that follow its comment, and the kind guard excludes only interstitials, so a paragraph is clamped like a line end.

name: max_blank_lines/blanks_before_a_paragraph_comment
why: Here the blanks are on the LineEnd ahead of the paragraph rather than on it.

name: max_blank_lines/interstitial_between_blank_runs
why: The interstitial is skipped by kind and could not carry blanks anyway — the model forbids them. The line ends either side of it are clamped.

name: max_blank_lines/in_super_fodder_is_out_of_reach
why: InSuper's in_fodder is one of the four slots pass::base never visits, so tk fmt leaves this run of blanks exactly as written. FixIndentation does reach it, because it is not an ASTPass and walks the tree itself.

name: max_blank_lines/index_id_fodder_is_out_of_reach
why: Index's right_bracket_fodder, doubling as the fodder before an identifier: the second of the two unvisited slots that can hold blanks.

name: max_blank_lines/super_index_id_fodder_is_reached
why: The contrast that makes the Index case a hole rather than a rule: base::super_index visits id_fodder unconditionally, so this one is clamped.

name: max_blank_lines/parameter_eq_fodder_is_reached_with_a_default
why: eq_fodder is visited only where there is a default — and without one there is no `=` for fodder to precede, which is why that unvisited slot is unobservable here.

name: max_blank_lines/tail_strict_fodder_is_reached
why: Same shape: tail_strict_fodder is skipped unless `tailstrict` is present, and without it the slot is empty. So only two of the four holes matter to this pass.

name: max_blank_lines/blanks_in_a_local_bind
why: A bind's eq_fodder, reached through base::local.

name: max_blank_lines/blanks_in_call_arguments
why: An argument's opening fodder and the fodder before the closing paren.

name: fix_newlines/array_expand_from_an_element
why: One element on a new line expands them all, and the close bracket too.

name: fix_newlines/array_expand_from_the_close_bracket
why: CloseFodder alone is enough to expand every element.

name: fix_newlines/array_stays_unexpanded
why: Nothing designated holds a newline, so nothing is added. No-op.

name: fix_newlines/array_shallow_over_a_nested_object
why: Upstream's own doc-comment example: the outer array stays unexpanded because the newlines are inside the braces, not between `[` and `{`.

name: fix_newlines/array_empty_with_a_newline
why: No elements, so only CloseFodder is consulted — and it already has a clean newline, so this is a no-op.

name: fix_newlines/array_element_after_an_interstitial
why: FodderEnsureCleanNewline appends to fodder ending in an interstitial rather than replacing it, so the comment keeps its place and the element moves below it.

name: fix_newlines/array_interstitials_only_do_not_count
why: FodderCountNewlines scores an interstitial 0, so a line full of them leaves the array unexpanded. No-op.

name: fix_newlines/array_paragraph_counts
why: A trailing `//` comment is a Paragraph, whose count is comment lines plus blanks and so is at least 1. The array expands.

name: fix_newlines/object_expand_from_a_field
why: Fodder1 of a non-first field carries the newline.

name: fix_newlines/object_expand_from_the_close_brace
why: CloseFodder alone expands every field.

name: fix_newlines/object_stays_unexpanded
why: No-op.

name: fix_newlines/object_field_str_reads_the_expression_fodder
why: objectFieldOpenFodder switches on the kind: an ObjectFieldStr has no Fodder1, so it reads openFodder(Expr1) instead. Get that wrong and an object of quoted fields never expands.

name: fix_newlines/object_field_str_mixed_with_an_id
why: One field of each kind, so both branches of objectFieldOpenFodder run over the same node.

name: fix_newlines/object_local_field
why: An ObjectLocal takes the Fodder1 branch.

name: fix_newlines/object_assert_field
why: So does an ObjectAssert.

name: fix_newlines/local_expand_from_the_first_bind
why: shouldExpand is computed over every bind including the first, but the rewrite skips i == 0 — so the first bind's newline expands the others while the first is left exactly as written.

name: fix_newlines/local_expand_from_a_later_bind
why: y's newline expands z; x is skipped by the i > 0 guard even though it has no newline of its own.

name: fix_newlines/local_single_bind_is_a_no_op
why: shouldExpand is true and the loop body never runs, because the only bind is i == 0. A no-op, and not the same kind of no-op as having nothing to expand.

name: fix_newlines/local_stays_unexpanded
why: No-op.

name: fix_newlines/parens_expand_from_the_inside
why: The inner expression's newline pulls the close paren onto its own line.

name: fix_newlines/parens_expand_from_the_close
why: And the reverse.

name: fix_newlines/parens_flat
why: No-op.

name: fix_newlines/params_near_parens_from_the_first
why: A newline before the first parameter sets shouldExpandNearParens only, so the close paren moves and `b` does not.

name: fix_newlines/params_between_from_a_later_one
why: A newline before a non-first parameter sets shouldExpandBetween only, so b and c expand and neither `a` nor the close paren does.

name: fix_newlines/params_near_parens_from_the_close
why: A newline before `)` is the other way into shouldExpandNearParens, and it expands the first parameter but not the second.

name: fix_newlines/params_both
why: Both flags set at once: everything expands.

name: fix_newlines/params_none
why: With no parameters the loops do nothing and only `r` is consulted — and it already has a clean newline. No-op.

name: fix_newlines/params_default_arg
why: NameFodder is what is measured, never EqFodder.

name: fix_newlines/args_positional_between
why: Upstream's `f(1, 2,` / `3)` example: the newline is between arguments, so they line up and the close paren stays put.

name: fix_newlines/args_positional_near_parens
why: Upstream's `foo(` / `1, 2, 3)` example: the close paren moves instead.

name: fix_newlines/args_named_between
why: The named loop reads NameFodder, and `first` is shared with the positional loop above it.

name: fix_newlines/args_named_only_first
why: With no positional arguments the first *named* one is what `first` protects.

name: fix_newlines/args_mixed_newline_before_a_named
why: `first` is consumed by the positional argument, so the named `a` counts as non-first and sets shouldExpandBetween. The positional stays.

name: fix_newlines/args_mixed_newline_before_the_positional
why: The mirror: the positional is first, so this is nearParens, and the named argument is not expanded.

name: fix_newlines/args_none
why: No arguments, so only `r` is consulted. No-op.

name: fix_newlines/array_comp_expand_from_the_for
why: ForFodder's newline expands the body, every spec and the close bracket.

name: fix_newlines/array_comp_expand_from_the_body
why: openFodder(Body) is the other trigger.

name: fix_newlines/array_comp_expand_from_an_if
why: shouldExpandSpec also reads each condition's IfFodder.

name: fix_newlines/array_comp_nested_for_expands_both
source:
[x for x in [1]
  for y in [2]]
why: The leftmost `for` is the outermost, so the newline here is on the inner spec; shouldExpandSpec recurses through Outer and ensureSpecExpanded then expands both.

name: fix_newlines/array_comp_flat
why: No-op.

name: fix_newlines/object_comp_expand
why: The object-comprehension path: fields, then the spec, then the brace.

name: fix_newlines/object_comp_flat
why: No-op.

name: indentation/already_correct
why: The case that matters most for a formatter that writes in place: a tk-fmt-clean file has to come back untouched. No-op.

name: indentation/tab_indented
why: The lexer counts a tab as 8, so this arrives as indent=8 and has to become 2. Indentation is the one thing the parse/unparse round trip does not regenerate for free.

name: indentation/over_indented
why: Six spaces down to two.

name: indentation/under_indented
why: Zero up to two.

name: indentation/nested_objects
why: Three levels, every one of them wrong, so each `base + Indent` step is observable separately.

name: indentation/array_lines_up_after_the_bracket
why: The first element is on the bracket's line, so newIndent lines up at the column after `[` rather than resetting to base + Indent.

name: indentation/array_resets_when_the_first_element_is_on_a_new_line
why: firstFodder starts with a LineEnd, so newIndent takes the reset branch and nothing lines up.

name: indentation/array_strong_indent
why: A later element preceded by a newline turns on strongIndent, so newIndentStrong makes the line-up column the new *base* as well — which changes what sub-expressions inside the elements indent from.

name: indentation/array_strong_indent_nested
why: strongIndent with sub-objects, which is where base != lineUp shows.

name: indentation/array_close_bracket_takes_the_base
why: fillLast gives the closing bracket's own element currIndent.base while every element before it gets newIndent.lineUp. Two answers in one fodder.

name: indentation/array_close_bracket_with_two_comments
why: Two paragraphs in CloseFodder, so setIndents's all-but-last split is observable: the first takes newIndent.lineUp and only the second takes currIndent.base.

name: indentation/apply_lines_up_under_the_paren
why: The `indent` struct's own doc example: at the `2` the indent is base 0, lineUp 11.

name: indentation/apply_resets_after_a_newline
why: firstFodder is the first argument's and it has a newline, so the arguments reset to base + Indent instead of lining up under the paren.

name: indentation/apply_strong_indent
why: A non-first argument with a newline selects newIndentStrong.

name: indentation/apply_named_args
why: firstFodder is taken from Named only when Positional is empty — the Positional loop runs second and overwrites it.

name: indentation/apply_mixed_args_first_fodder
why: With both kinds present the positional wins firstFodder, and `first` is shared across the two strongIndent loops.

name: indentation/apply_close_paren_takes_the_base
why: Apply's fillLast ends on currIndent.base where params ends on currIndent.lineUp. The pair is easy to transpose and this snippet is what tells them apart.

name: indentation/apply_tailstrict
why: TailStrictFodder is filled at currIndent.base, and the column then advances by 10.

name: indentation/apply_chained
why: Apply is left-recursive, so separateToken is false and align carries the target's own fodder rather than the node's.

name: indentation/params_close_paren_takes_the_line_up
why: The other half of the Apply pairing above: params's fillLast ends on currIndent.lineUp.

name: indentation/params_default_arg_has_no_spacing
why: EqFodder is filled with crowded and separateToken both false and the column advances by exactly 1 — `x=e`, no spaces around it.

name: indentation/params_empty
why: With no parameters firstInside is fodderR, so newIndent is computed from the very fodder fillLast is about to rewrite.

name: indentation/binary_align_op_on_the_first_line
why: OpFodder has no newline but the right side does, so alignStrong is selected rather than align.

name: indentation/binary_align_op_on_the_second_line
why: The other half of the same condition: here OpFodder carries the newline.

name: indentation/binary_no_newlines
why: align, taking its reset branch, which returns `old` unchanged. No-op.

name: indentation/binary_chain_keeps_one_indent
why: Upstream deliberately does not compute a new indent for the right side, so a chain does not stair-step.

name: indentation/binary_deep_left
why: Left-recursive through two Binary nodes, so openFodder has to reach the leftmost leaf.

name: indentation/conditional_uses_the_base
source:
if a
then b
else c
why: ThenFodder and ElseFodder are filled at currIndent.base, not lineUp, while each branch gets its own newIndent at column + 1.

name: indentation/conditional_nested
source:
if a then
if b then
c else
d else
e
why: Nested conditionals, where base and lineUp diverge.

name: indentation/conditional_no_else
why: BranchFalse absent, so ElseFodder is never filled.

name: indentation/local_binds_line_up
why: newIndent comes from the *first* bind's VarFodder at column + 1, and every later bind is filled from it.

name: indentation/local_bind_body_indents_from_the_bind
why: newIndent2 is computed with `newIndent` as its old rather than currIndent — the one place in this pass that chains instead of resetting from the node.

name: indentation/local_close_fodder_takes_the_base
why: fillLast on a bind's CloseFodder: newIndent2.lineUp for all but the last element and currIndent.base for the last.

name: indentation/local_function_bind
why: A bind's Fun goes through params with `newIndent`, not currIndent.

name: indentation/local_body_takes_the_outer_indent
why: The body is visited with currIndent, so a `local` at the top of a file does not indent what follows it.

name: indentation/object_field_id
why: The ObjectFieldID branch fills Fodder1 at the `newIndent` int, which is the object's newIndent.lineUp — not at currIndent.base.

name: indentation/object_local_field_uses_curr_indent
why: ObjectLocal fills at currIndent.lineUp where ObjectFieldID fills at the `newIndent` int. They happen to agree here, which is exactly why a transposition would survive most inputs.

name: indentation/object_field_expr
why: The computed-name branch: Expr1 is visited with currIndent and Fodder2 is filled at newIndent.

name: indentation/object_field_str
why: ObjectFieldStr has no Fodder1 at all; the name expression is visited with currIndent and carries the crowded flag instead.

name: indentation/object_assert_visits_the_condition_with_curr_indent
why: The oddity: newIndent2 is computed from openFodder(Expr2) at column + 1, then Expr2 is visited with **currIndent** and only Expr3 gets newIndent2. The top-level Assert node visits its condition with the new indent, so the two disagree.

name: indentation/object_method
why: fieldParams runs params with currIndent, inside a field whose own fills use the newIndent int.

name: indentation/object_close_brace_takes_the_base
why: fillLast on CloseFodder, with PadObjects true so the line-up column is one past the brace.

name: indentation/object_pad_objects_shifts_the_line_up
why: PadObjects is true under DefaultOptions, so the first field is crowded and newColumn is incremented before newIndent is taken.

name: indentation/object_empty_with_a_newline
why: No fields, so firstFodder is CloseFodder and `fields` does nothing.

name: indentation/object_comp
why: ObjectComp passes crowded=true to fillLast unconditionally, where Object passes len(Fields) > 0.

name: indentation/array_comp
why: specs walks Outer first, so the fors come out in source order.

name: indentation/array_comp_nested_for
source:
[
x
for x in [1]
for y in [2]
]
why: Two specs, and the recursion in specs is what puts them at one indent rather than stair-stepping.

name: indentation/comp_if_revisits_the_for_expression
why: UPSTREAM BUG, reproduced. The conditions loop in `specs` computes its indent from openFodder(spec.Expr) and then calls Visit(spec.Expr) — the `for` expression, not cond.Expr. So this array is indented twice, at two different columns, and the second answer wins.

name: indentation/comp_if_condition_is_never_visited
why: The other half of the same bug: cond.Expr is never visited at all, so the six spaces before `true` survive untouched. Only IfFodder is filled.

name: indentation/parens_are_strong
why: Parens is the only node that calls newIndentStrong unconditionally, so everything inside indents from the column after `(`.

name: indentation/parens_close_takes_the_base
why: fillLast again: newIndent.lineUp, then currIndent.base for the last element.

name: indentation/index_by_id
why: The Id branch takes newIndent *from* RightBracketFodder and then fills that same slot from it, so the order of those two lines matters.

name: indentation/index_by_expression
why: The bracket branch, whose fillLast ends on currIndent.base.

name: indentation/super_index_by_id
why: The same doubled slot under a different name — IDFodder here.

name: indentation/super_index_by_expression
why: And its bracket branch.

name: indentation/in_super_is_reached_here
why: InFodder and SuperFodder are two of the four slots pass::base never visits — but FixIndentation is not an ASTPass, so it fills both. That asymmetry is why a comment there survives EnforceCommentStyle and is still re-indented.

name: indentation/slice_begin_and_end
why: EndColonFodder supplies newIndent when EndIndex is present.

name: indentation/slice_step_without_an_end
why: Step with no EndIndex: the EndColonFodder branch runs inside the Step branch instead, and newIndent is assigned there.

name: indentation/slice_bare_colon
why: All three absent, which is the fourth and otherwise unreachable branch.

name: indentation/slice_all_three
why: newIndent is reassigned as the branches run, so the step indents from the end index's answer.

name: indentation/slice_right_bracket_is_never_filled
why: A hole: the Slice case fills LeftBracketFodder and each colon's fodder and never touches RightBracketFodder, so a newline before a slice's `]` keeps whatever indent it was lexed with. Every other bracketed node calls fillLast there.

name: indentation/unary
why: newIndent from the operand's fodder at the column after the operator.

name: indentation/unary_of_dollar_is_crowded
why: leftRecursiveDeep(Expr) is a Dollar, so the operand is visited as crowded — the one place this pass asks what the leftmost leaf *is* rather than what fodder it holds.

name: indentation/unary_of_a_var_is_not_crowded
why: The contrast: not a Dollar, so crowded is false and the column model differs by one.

name: indentation/error_expression
why: column += 5, then newIndent at column + 1 for the space after `error`.

name: indentation/assert_expression
why: The top-level Assert: Cond does get newIndent here, unlike the object assert above, and Rest is visited with currIndent.

name: indentation/assert_without_a_message
why: Message absent, so ColonFodder is never filled.

name: indentation/import
why: column += 6, and the file is then visited as an ordinary node.

name: indentation/importstr
why: column += 9, which importbin shares and import does not.

name: indentation/importbin
why: The third keyword width.

name: indentation/function_body
why: The body's newIndent is taken at column + 1, after params has advanced the column past the closing paren.

name: indentation/apply_brace
why: ApplyBrace aligns on the left operand and visits the right as crowded.

name: indentation/block_string_indents_are_rewritten
why: StringBlock is the only case where this pass edits the AST rather than fodder: BlockIndent becomes base + Indent spaces and BlockTermIndent becomes base spaces, whatever the author wrote. It also *assigns* the column rather than adding to it.

name: indentation/block_string_at_the_top_level
why: base is 0 here, so BlockTermIndent becomes the empty string.

name: indentation/block_string_nested_deeper
why: base is further along by this point, so the two indents come out larger.

name: indentation/string_column_counts_bytes
why: StringSingle advances the column by 2 + len(Value) in *bytes*, so three two-byte characters count six. The next element lines up from that.

name: indentation/verbatim_string_column_counts_runes
why: The verbatim branches loop over runes instead, adding 1 each — so the same three characters count three. Bytes there, runes here, in one match.

name: indentation/verbatim_string_doubles_quotes
why: A quote inside a verbatim string costs 2 columns, because the unparser will write it doubled.

name: indentation/interstitial_advances_the_column
why: fillLast models the unparser's column bookkeeping: an interstitial adds its comment's byte length, plus one for the space when crowded.

name: indentation/interstitial_then_line_end
why: A LineEnd after an interstitial *assigns* the column from the indent, discarding everything the interstitial added.

name: indentation/final_fodder_is_zeroed
why: VisitFile ends with setIndents(finalFodder, 0, 0), so a comment after the last token is flushed left however it was written.

name: indentation/literal_widths
why: The four fixed column widths — 4, 5, 4, and the number's original string.

name: indentation/deeply_mixed
why: One snippet through most of the branches at once, as an integration case rather than a unit one.

name: fix_parens/single
why: One pair of parens is not redundant. The no-op is graded too.

name: fix_parens/double
why: The pass exists for this: the inner Parens is spliced out and the outer keeps its place.

name: fix_parens/triple
why: The `if` is not a loop, so exactly one level goes: P1.Inner becomes P3 and the walk moves on to P3, which has a literal inside it. So `jsonnetfmt` is not a fixed point here either -- formatting the answer again removes another pair.

name: fix_parens/quad
why: Four levels halve to two: P1 absorbs P2, then the walk reaches P3 and it absorbs P4.

name: fix_parens/double_inner_open_comment
why: The comment between the two `(` is the *inner* Parens' own fodder, and FodderMoveFront puts it in front of the outer's -- so it ends up outside the surviving paren.

name: fix_parens/double_outer_and_inner_open_comment
why: Both slots are occupied, so the move concatenates and the two comments come out in the other order.

name: fix_parens/double_close_comments
why: The close-fodder move, with both slots occupied.

name: fix_parens/double_inner_close_only
why: The inner close fodder is empty, so the outer's is left as it was. A move from an empty slot is the common case.

name: fix_parens/double_multiline
why: A line end before the inner `(` and before the outer `)`, so both moves carry a LineEnd.

name: fix_parens/double_newline_between_opens
why: Only the open-fodder move carries anything.

name: fix_parens/double_line_comment_between_opens
why: A paragraph moved into empty fodder, which is where FodderAppend's synthetic LineEnd rule can fire.

name: fix_parens/double_comment_both_sides_of_seam
why: Concat with a paragraph on each side of the seam: the invariant is enforced at exactly one element.

name: fix_parens/double_blank_lines_between_opens
why: Blanks are a count on the moved element, not separate elements.

name: fix_parens/inner_not_parens
why: The outer's inner is a Binary whose left happens to be a Parens, which is not the shape this pass matches. A no-op.

name: fix_parens/parens_in_binary_left
why: The redundant pair is not the root, so the collapse has to happen wherever the walk finds it.

name: fix_parens/parens_in_binary_right
why: The same, on the other side.

name: fix_parens/in_object_field
why: Reached through the object-field hook rather than from the root.

name: fix_parens/in_array
why: Two collapses in one file.

name: fix_parens/apply_target
why: The Parens is an Apply's target, so the enclosing node is left-recursive.

name: fix_parens/index_target
why: openFodder on a Parens is its own fodder -- Parens is not left-recursive -- even where its parent is.

name: fix_parens/double_around_object
why: The inner expression is an Object, which is what the plus-object passes at step 7 will be looking at.

name: fix_parens/nested_deeper_inside
why: The outer pair collapses and the unrelated `(2)` deeper in is untouched.

name: fix_parens/three_opens_with_comments
why: The collapse takes the middle Parens' comment outward and leaves the innermost one where it is.

name: fix_parens/double_in_local_bind
why: Through the local hook.

name: fix_parens/double_in_function_default
why: Through the parameters hook, which only descends into a default that exists.

name: remove_plus_object/var_plus_object
why: The pass's whole purpose: a Var on the left and an Object on the right becomes an ApplyBrace, so the `+` is not written.

name: remove_plus_object/index_plus_object
why: An Index on the left is the other accepted shape.

name: remove_plus_object/bracket_index_plus_object
why: The bracket form of Index, which is the same Go type.

name: remove_plus_object/dotted_chain_plus_object
why: An Index whose target is an Index.

name: remove_plus_object/index_of_apply_plus_object
why: The test is on the *outermost* node of the left side, so an Index over an Apply is accepted although an Apply is not.

name: remove_plus_object/object_plus_object
why: NOT rewritten. Upstream restricts the left side to a Var or an Index -- 'Could relax this to allow more ASTs on the LHS but this seems OK for now' -- so this is the negative case that says the restriction is real.

name: remove_plus_object/apply_plus_object
why: NOT rewritten: an Apply on the left is not accepted.

name: remove_plus_object/parens_plus_object
why: NOT rewritten: Parens is not Var, whatever it wraps.

name: remove_plus_object/slice_plus_object
why: NOT rewritten: ast.Slice is a different type from ast.Index, and only Index is accepted.

name: remove_plus_object/super_index_plus_object
why: NOT rewritten: ast.SuperIndex is its own type too.

name: remove_plus_object/self_plus_object
why: NOT rewritten.

name: remove_plus_object/dollar_plus_object
why: NOT rewritten.

name: remove_plus_object/var_plus_array
why: NOT rewritten: the right side has to be an Object.

name: remove_plus_object/var_plus_object_comp
why: NOT rewritten: ast.ObjectComp is a different type from ast.Object, so a comprehension keeps its `+`.

name: remove_plus_object/var_plus_parenthesised_object
why: NOT rewritten: the right side is a Parens.

name: remove_plus_object/var_minus_object
why: NOT rewritten: the operator has to be `+`.

name: remove_plus_object/var_mult_object
why: NOT rewritten.

name: remove_plus_object/op_fodder_interstitial
why: The comment is the Binary's OpFodder, and the `+` it sat in front of is about to disappear -- so it moves to the front of the object's own fodder.

name: remove_plus_object/op_fodder_line_end
why: The line end before the `+` becomes the line end before the `{`. This is the shape the docsonnet corpus file has.

name: remove_plus_object/op_fodder_and_object_fodder
why: Both slots hold a LineEnd, so the move goes through FodderAppend's merge rule rather than a plain concatenation.

name: remove_plus_object/op_fodder_comment_both
why: A comment on each side of the seam.

name: remove_plus_object/object_fodder_only
why: The comment is after the `+`, so it is the object's fodder already and the (empty) move changes nothing.

name: remove_plus_object/chain_left_converts
why: Left-associative, so the outer Binary's left is a Binary and is refused while the inner one converts. The answer is `a { b: 1 } + { c: 2 }`, which is exactly what the docsonnet golden shows.

name: remove_plus_object/chain_right_is_not_object
why: The outer is refused twice over; the inner still converts.

name: remove_plus_object/already_apply_brace
why: Already an ApplyBrace, so there is nothing to do. The pass never looks at one.

name: remove_plus_object/in_object_field
why: Through the object-field hook.

name: remove_plus_object/in_array
why: Through the array hook.

name: remove_plus_object/in_local_bind
why: Through the local hook.

name: remove_plus_object/nested_rhs_also_converts
why: The walk continues into the replacement's children, so both convert.

name: remove_plus_object/empty_object
why: An empty Object is still an Object.

name: remove_plus_object/object_with_local
why: An object whose first field is a local, so the replacement has to keep the field list intact.

name: remove_plus_object/hidden_field_object
why: A hidden field, to pin that only the node kinds are looked at.

name: add_plus_object/top_level
why: The root has a nil parent, so no parens: BaseContext returns an empty passCtx.

name: add_plus_object/three
why: Two ApplyBraces. The outer becomes a Binary with no parens; the inner is then that Binary's *left*, and `+` is left-associative, so it needs none either.

name: add_plus_object/var_brace
why: The commonest real shape, and the one RemovePlusObject produces.

name: add_plus_object/apply_target
why: Apply binds tighter than `+`, so the target position needs parens.

name: add_plus_object/apply_positional_arg
why: An argument is delimited by the parens that are already there, so none are added.

name: add_plus_object/apply_named_arg
why: The same, reached through the named-argument slot.

name: add_plus_object/apply_tailstrict
why: The tailstrict fodder slot is only visited when the keyword is there, so this exercises the branch.

name: add_plus_object/index_target_dot
why: Upstream's own regression case: without the parens the formatted expression is a runtime error rather than a differently-spelled program.

name: add_plus_object/index_target_bracket
why: The bracket form of the same.

name: add_plus_object/index_expression
why: The index expression is delimited by its brackets, so no parens.

name: add_plus_object/index_target_chained
why: The ApplyBrace is the target of the *inner* Index, which is where the parens go.

name: add_plus_object/slice_target
why: ast.Slice is not in upstream's switch, so it takes the default branch and NO parens are added -- although Slice binds as tightly as Index. Recorded because it is what the reference implementation does.

name: add_plus_object/binary_left_plus
why: On the left of a `+`: 6 < 6 is false, so no parens -- left-associativity makes the flattened form parse the same.

name: add_plus_object/binary_right_plus
why: On the right of a `+`: 6 <= 6 is true, so parens. The asymmetry is the associativity.

name: add_plus_object/binary_left_minus
why: `-` has the same precedence as `+`, so the left side needs nothing.

name: add_plus_object/binary_right_minus
why: And the right side does.

name: add_plus_object/binary_left_mult
why: `*` binds tighter (5 < 6), so the left side needs parens as well.

name: add_plus_object/binary_right_mult
why: And so does the right.

name: add_plus_object/binary_left_or
why: `||` binds looser (14), so neither side needs parens.

name: add_plus_object/binary_right_or
why: The looser operator on the right: 14 <= 6 is false.

name: add_plus_object/binary_left_in
why: `in` as an ordinary binary operator, precedence 8.

name: add_plus_object/binary_right_in
why: The right of an `in`: still no parens, because `+` binds tighter than `in` and the parse is unchanged.

name: add_plus_object/unary_plus
why: Upstream's own case. The parse is `+(implicit-plus 42 {b:2})`, and explicit `+` binds looser than unary `+`, so parens are needed to keep it. The expression does not evaluate; it still has to format.

name: add_plus_object/unary_minus
why: The same for unary `-`.

name: add_plus_object/unary_not
why: And for `!`: the branch is a constant comparison, 4 < 6, so every Unary parent needs parens.

name: add_plus_object/unary_bitwise_not
why: And for `~`.

name: add_plus_object/in_super
why: InSuper's own branch, which compares precedence(in) <= precedence(+) -- 8 <= 6 -- and so is always false. No parens, and that is correct: `+` binds tighter than `in`.

name: add_plus_object/in_object_field
why: An Object parent takes the default branch.

name: add_plus_object/in_array
why: So does an Array.

name: add_plus_object/in_local_bind
why: So does a Local.

name: add_plus_object/local_body
why: The body slot of the same Local.

name: add_plus_object/conditional_branches
source: if c then { a: 1 } { b: 2 } else { c: 1 } { d: 2 }
why: Both branches, and a Conditional parent needs no parens.

name: add_plus_object/conditional_cond
why: The condition slot.

name: add_plus_object/error_expr
why: An Error parent.

name: add_plus_object/assert_cond
why: An Assert's condition.

name: add_plus_object/assert_message
why: An Assert's message, which is only visited when it is there.

name: add_plus_object/function_body
why: A Function parent.

name: add_plus_object/function_default
why: A parameter default, reached through the parameters hook.

name: add_plus_object/for_spec_expr
why: The `in` expression of a comprehension, reached through for_spec.

name: add_plus_object/if_spec_expr
source: [x for x in y if { a: 1 } { b: 2 }]
why: A comprehension's condition, reached through the same hook.

name: add_plus_object/object_comp_field
source: { [k]: { a: 1 } { b: 2 } for k in y }
why: An ObjectComp parent.

name: add_plus_object/field_name_expr
why: A computed field name, which is the FieldExpr branch of object_field.

name: add_plus_object/already_parenthesised
why: The inner ApplyBrace's parent is a Parens, which takes the default branch -- so the parens already in the source are the ones that stay.

name: add_plus_object/parens_inner
why: A Parens parent on its own.

name: add_plus_object/nested_under_inserted_parens
why: The outer ApplyBrace is an Index target and gets parens; the *replacement* node is handed down as the parent, so the inner ApplyBrace sees the new Parens rather than the Binary, and then the Binary, and needs nothing.

name: add_plus_object/apply_of_index_target
why: Upstream's `implicit-plus-apply`: the ApplyBrace is the target of an Index which is itself the target of an Apply.

name: add_plus_object/index_then_apply_brace
why: An ApplyBrace whose left is an Index, which is the shape RemovePlusObject produces from `a.b + { c: 1 }`.

name: add_plus_object/object_fodder_before_brace
why: The right-hand object carries a LineEnd in its own fodder, which the replacement must leave alone.

name: add_plus_object/super_index_target
why: A SuperIndex on the left of an implicit plus.

name: add_plus_object/deep_chain_in_field
why: Two ApplyBraces under an Index under an object field.
